theme: Send out your light and your truth
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 43. It is the second half of the poem you began yesterday. Notice how the psalmist asks for light and truth, and how he moves toward the altar of God.
settingTheScene: Psalm 43 has no title in the Hebrew, and many manuscripts join it with Psalm 42 as a single poem. It shares the same refrain. The first psalm described the longing, and this psalm makes the request. The psalmist is surrounded by deceitful people, and he asks God to vindicate him and bring him back to worship.
observation: “Vindicate me, O God, and defend my cause against an ungodly people” (v. 1).
“From the deceitful and unjust man deliver me!” (v. 1).
“For you are the God in whom I take refuge; why have you rejected me?” (v. 2).
“Why do I go about mourning because of the oppression of the enemy?” (v. 2).
“Send out your light and your truth; let them lead me; let them bring me to your holy hill and to your dwelling!” (v. 3).
“Then I will go to the altar of God, to God my exceeding joy” (v. 4).
“And I will praise you with the lyre, O God, my God” (v. 4).
“Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation and my God” (v. 5).
interpretation:
Where Psalm 42 was a lament, Psalm 43 is a petition. The psalmist asks God to be his advocate. He is in the middle of a case, and he wants God to judge between him and his enemies. He does not take revenge. He asks for vindication, for God to set things right.

Verse 2 repeats the question from Psalm 42:9: “Why have you rejected me?” The psalmist is honest about how it feels. He knows that God is his refuge, and yet he feels abandoned. The two statements sit side by side. This is not contradiction. It is the real experience of believers who have faith but not yet sight.

Verse 3 is the center of the poem: “Send out your light and your truth.” The psalmist treats God’s light and truth as if they were two messengers who could be dispatched to lead him. They are personified, almost like angels. Light shows the way, and truth keeps him from deception. He needs both. When surrounded by lies, he asks for truth. When in darkness, he asks for light.

Where do they lead? To God’s holy hill, his dwelling place. The psalmist’s goal is not just rescue but worship. He wants to return to the altar and to “God my exceeding joy.” Literally, “the gladness of my joy.” God himself is the source of the psalmist’s deepest happiness. He wants to be where God is.

The refrain returns for a third time. It is almost stubborn. “Hope in God; for I shall again praise him.” The “again” is important. The psalmist is confident that the dry time will end and that praise will return.
connection: Jesus is the light and truth that God sent. “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12) and “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). “Grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17). Hebrews 10:19-22 shows that through Christ we have access to God’s presence, the “altar” the psalmist longed for. Jesus is our advocate with the Father (1 John 2:1).
application:
Pray verse 3 for a specific situation: “Send out your light and your truth.”

Ask God to lead you to his dwelling, to a deeper experience of worship.

Say the refrain aloud, “Hope in God,” and add “for I shall again praise him.”
prayerPrompts: Ask God to send out his light and truth to lead you.
Tell him that he is your exceeding joy.
Tell your soul to hope in him.
